## Part 1 -- Multiple Testing

The code below simulates sampling 100 individuals with unrelated explanatory (X) and response (Y) variables, conducting linear models, and returning p values for 200 tests. You will need to edit it to set a seed.


```{r, eval=F}

set.seed() ##pick a number to set your seed here

doExp <- function(i){
  myX <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myY <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myModel = lm(myY ~ myX) #fit linear model
  myP = summary(myModel)$coefficients[2,4] #get p value
  return(myP)
}

nTests=200

simulated_pvalues <- sapply(1:nTests, doExp) ## run doExp 1000 times
```

**1a) Calculate the family-wide error rate for an alpha value of 0.05 and 200 tests using the formula from the lecture and the notes.**

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
1 - (1-0.05)^200
```

**1b) Run the simulations in the code above and calculate how many of the simulated p values are below 0.05. How does this compare to your expectation from part a?**

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
set.seed(31) ##pick a number to set your seed here

doExp <- function(i){
  myX <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myY <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myModel = lm(myY ~ myX) #fit linear model
  myP = summary(myModel)$coefficients[2,4] #get p value
  return(myP)
}

nTests=200

simulated_pvalues <- sapply(1:nTests, doExp) ## run doExp 1000 times

sum(simulated_pvalues<0.05)
#there were 4 significant results at alpha=0.05, matching my expectation that I would get at least one significant result
```


**1c) Calculate the appropriate Bonferroni cut-off for 200 tests. How many of the simulated p values are below this cut off?**

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}
bonf = 0.05/200
bonf

sum(simulated_pvalues<bonf)
#none
```

**1d) Use the `p.adjust()` function to calculate an fdr corresponding each simulated p value. What is the lowest fdr? How many fdr valures are below 0.05?**

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}
fdrs <- p.adjust(simulated_pvalues, method="fdr") #calculate FDRs

sum(simulated_pvalues<bonf)
```

**1e) Which method do you think worked best for controlling the family-wise error rate? Why?**


**2a) Edit the code above so that the response variable Y is a function of the explanatory variable X. Pick any `b_0`, but set `b_1 = 2` and set the standard deviation of the residuals to `3`. If you get stuck, check the starter code from the simulation activity from last week. Then, rerun the simulations 200 times to generate a new set of p values.**

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
set.seed(31) ##pick a number to set your seed here
b_0=5
b_1 = 2
mysd = 3

doExp2 <- function(i){
  myX <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myY <- b_0+b_1*myX+rnorm(n=100,mean=0,sd=mysd)
  myModel = lm(myY ~ myX) #fit linear model
  myP = summary(myModel)$coefficients[2,4] #get p value
  return(myP)
}

nTests=200

simulated_pvalues2 <- sapply(1:nTests, doExp2) ## run doExp2 200 times
```

**2b) Make a histogram of the simulated p values and compare to a histogram of the p values from part 1. **

```{r, echo=F,eval=F}
hist(simulated_pvalues)
hist(simulated_pvalues2)

```

**2c) How many of the simulated p values are below 0.05? Is this more or less than part 1?**

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}

sum(simulated_pvalues2<0.05) #more
```

**2d) How many of the simulated p values are below the Bonferroni cut-off?**

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}

sum(simulated_pvalues2<0.05/200) 
```


**2e) Use the p.adjust() function to calculate an fdr corresponding each simulated p value. What is the lowest fdr? How many fdr valures are below 0.05?**


```{r, echo=F, eval=F}
fdrs <- p.adjust(simulated_pvalues2, method="fdr") #calculate FDRs

sum(fdrs<0.05)

min(fdrs)
```

## Part 2 -- Genome Wide Association Studies.

In this part of the lab you will examine outputs of a GWAS analysis and link it to a general linear model. Actually running a GWAS can be a huge pain because the data files are large and often use irritating formats (Emily spent a few hours wrangling files before abandoning the idea of you all running your own GWASs on your laptops). Instead, you'll be using the results of a GWAS that Emily has already run for you (you can see the code here: https://github.com/bobvanburen/PLB812_F25_GWAS/blob/main/gwas-lab-2025.ipynb)

The species: *Arabidopsis thaliana*, a cute little herbaceous weed found all over Europe, often in disturbed habitats. Because *A. thaliana* are selfers, individuals are almost always homozygous, so their numeric genotypes will either be 0 or 2.

The trait: Flowering time, measured in a growth chamber. This trait is really important shaping plant fitness. It is measured as days to flower ('dtf').

First, here are results for a GWAS with a mixed model. The code below loads in the results as a data table. Some of the files are quite large, so let Emily know if you have trouble loading them into R and she can send you smaller files.

```{r, eval=F}
mixedGwas <- read.table('fl-mixed.assoc.txt', header=T)
```

**3a) Make a histogram of the pvalues (p_lrt) with 100 or more bins. **

**3b) Use p.adjust() to calculate an fdr (I suggest using p_lrt as the p value input). How many SNPs fall below an fdr of 0.05? How does this compare to the number of SNPs with a p value of 0.05?**

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
fdrs <- p.adjust(mixedGwas$p_lrt, method='fdr')

sum(fdrs < 0.05)

sum(mixedGwas$p_lrt < 0.05)
```

Now, let's look at some of the data the underlies this variation.

We'll start with a random SNP that didn't affect the trait in the GWAS, Chr5_19380396. The code below looks at the GWAS results for this SNP. It also loads data for the phenotype and genotype at this SNP for every individual in the experiment.

```{r, eval=F}

snp1 <- read.table(snp1_link, header=T)

```

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}
modelsnp1 <- lm(dtf~genotype, data=snp1)
summary(modelsnp1)
```

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
library(vcfR) #library to read in vcf
# read in polymorphism data about this snp
mysnp <- read.vcfR('Chr5_19380396.vcf')

# this is a function to calculate genotype numeric scores from the vcf

sum_genotype <- function(geno_col) {
  sapply(geno_col, function(gt) {
    if (is.na(gt) || gt == "./.") return(NA)  # Handle missing
    alleles <- unlist(strsplit(gt, "/"))      # Split by "/"
    sum(as.numeric(alleles))                  # Sum the two numbers
  })
}

## this is a function to deal with the weird ecotype names
extract_first_number <- function(col) {
  sapply(col, function(x) {
    strsplit(x, "_")[[1]][1] |> as.numeric()
  })
}

Z <- vcfR2tidy(mysnp, format_fields = "GT") #extract the genotype data from the vcf
genoDf <- data.frame(Z$gt) # turn into a data frame
genoDf$genotype = sapply(genoDf$gt_GT, sum_genotype) #turn to a numeric genotype
genoDf$FID = sapply(genoDf$Indiv, extract_first_number) #fix the genotype id

traits <- read.table('phenotypes.pheno', header=T) #read in trait data
mergedData <- dplyr::inner_join(genoDf, traits, by="FID") # merge in the phenotypes
outData = data.frame(mergedData$genotype, mergedData$DTF1)
names(outData) = c('genotype', 'dtf')
write.table(outData,file='~/Documents/msu-eeb830831-quarto/data/Chr5_19380396.txt', row.names=F, quote=F)


mysnp <- read.vcfR('Chr5_18590501.vcf')


Z <- vcfR2tidy(mysnp, format_fields = "GT")
genoDf <- data.frame(Z$gt)
genoDf$genotype = sapply(genoDf$gt_GT, sum_genotype) #turn to a numeric genotype
genoDf$FID = sapply(genoDf$Indiv, extract_first_number) #fix the genotype id

## merge in the phenos

mergedData <- dplyr::inner_join(genoDf, traits, by="FID")
outData = data.frame(mergedData$genotype, mergedData$DTF1)
names(outData) = c('genotype', 'dtf')
write.table(outData,file='~/Documents/msu-eeb830831-quarto/data/Chr5_18590501.txt', row.names=F, quote=F)


```
